title: Not even a thorn bush (Exodus Rabbah 2:5)
hookLine: God speaks from a thorn bush to show no place is empty of the Presence
tomorrow: Moses asks God's name. why does the answer keep changing?

cards: Run a thumb along a blackberry cane or a rose stem and you remember fast: thorns don't look like much until they're in your skin.
Moses is out in the wilderness with his father-in-law's flock when "the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush." Not a cedar. Not a palm.
A scrubby thorn bush. Someone asked the rabbis: why that one?

teach.b: Exodus Rabbah keeps the question and says who asked it: someone from outside the faith, curious, asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha why God would speak to Moses from a thorn bush.

teach.h: NO PLACE EMPTY OF THE PRESENCE.
teach.b: The question came from outside, and it got a straight answer: to teach you that no place is empty of the Presence, not even a thorn bush. The midrash gathers other readings too.
One: the thorn bush is the lowliest of plants, and the people in Egypt were low, so God came down to where they were.
The psalm says it: "I will be with him in trouble." Another notices how a thorn bush works.
A hand slides in easily, but pull it out and the thorns catch, and the midrash compares that to getting into Egypt, and trying to get out.
Every reading lands in the same place. The Presence doesn't wait for beautiful places. It speaks from the scratchy, the stuck, the low.
And the bush burns and isn't burned up: the thorns stay thorns, and the fire is in them anyway.

how: Exodus Rabbah is studied with the Torah portion Shemot, where Moses meets God at the bush; this answer is a much-quoted teaching about God's nearness in hard places.

games.q: what does “not even a thorn bush” mean?
o: a warning that God is hard to reach
a hedge planted to keep strangers away
even the scratchy places hold God's Presence

games.q: the readings of the bush — tap the pairs.
p: no place is empty of the Presence
God comes down to the low
easy in, hard to pull out

s: the bush was a grand, beautiful tree
it was a thorn bush, and that's the point.
in the midrash, the question comes from someone outside the faith
and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha gives a straight answer.
holy things happen only in holy places
not even a thorn bush is empty of the Presence.

games.q: your little sister asks: is God at the hospital where grandma is, or only at synagogue? what does the thorn bush let you say?
o: no place is empty of God, the midrash says, not even a hospital.
God is mostly at synagogue; hospitals are for the doctors.
nobody can know where God is, so it's better not to ask.
games.why: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: no place is empty of the Presence, not even a thorn bush.

practice: Find something rough within reach: bark, a brick, the bristles of a brush, the sole of a shoe. Rest your fingertips on it, gently, and feel every snag.
Let it stand for one thorny thing in your week, and keep your hand there, not pulling away, with the words: not even a thorn bush.

wordCard.voice: Not even a thorn bush: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's answer in Exodus Rabbah. No place is empty of the Presence, not even the scratchy one.

orig.note: Hebrew: the thorn bush of Exodus 3, where the midrash finds the Presence.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: not even a thorn bush, because the fire was in the thorns. That's fifteen seventy-nine.

sources.ref: Exodus Rabbah 2:5 (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: no place is empty of the Shekhinah, not even a thorn bush; other readings of the sneh)
